linkedin.title: Most people consume news by accident, not by design.
linkedin.body:
We scroll through social feeds or click on whatever happens to be trending. The result is a chaotic mix of information that often leaves us feeling overwhelmed and under-informed. We end up knowing a little bit about everything, but rarely enough about the things that actually matter to our lives or our work.

True information literacy isn't about reading more. It is about reading better. When you filter out the noise and focus on the stories that align with your genuine interests, you stop reacting to the news cycle and start understanding it. You move from passive consumption to active learning.

This is where AI changes the game. It isn't about creating echo chambers or hiding opposing views. It is about efficiency. Good technology should act as a curator, not a filter bubble. It should help you surface the deep-dive reporting, the niche industry updates, and the global context you would otherwise miss in the flood of daily headlines.

Staying informed shouldn't feel like a second job. It should be a seamless part of your day that actually adds value rather than just taking up your time.

reels.title: A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human
reels.hook: A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human

beats.caption: A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human
We thought dinosaurs were cold-blooded.
beats.narration: We always assumed dinosaurs were cold-blooded reptiles. Turns out that is completely wrong.

beats.caption: A 66-million-year-old tooth changed everything.
beats.narration: New evidence from a 66 million year old fossilized tooth has changed everything.

beats.caption: Its body heat was shockingly familiar.
beats.detail: Compare the T. rex to a human.
beats.narration: The chemical data shows the T. rex maintained a temperature nearly identical to our own.

beats.caption: It stayed at 97 degrees.
beats.narration: It hovered right around 97 degrees Fahrenheit.

beats.caption: This warm-blooded trait was a survival hack.
beats.detail: It explains how they stayed active.
beats.narration: Being warm-blooded gave the predator the energy it needed to hunt and survive in cold climates.

beats.caption: It proves they were far more active.
beats.detail: A massive predator always ready to move.
beats.narration: This confirms the T. rex was a highly active hunter, not some sluggish reptile.

beats.caption: Get the full story at headlinne.com.
beats.narration: For more science stories like this, check out headlinne.com.

story_card.headline: Use FaceTime on Android or Windows
story_card.standfirst: You do not need an Apple device to jump on a FaceTime call anymore.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text: You can now join FaceTime calls from Android phones or Windows computers.

steps.label: How we got here
steps.text: Apple opened up the service, allowing non-Apple users to connect via a browser link.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.text: It breaks down the walled garden, making it easier to chat with friends on any device.

steps.label: What to watch
steps.text: Note that this is not the full experience, just a way to join existing calls.

story_card.caption:
How to join a FaceTime call on Android or Windows devices.

FaceTime is no longer limited to Apple hardware. While you cannot host a call from these devices, you can easily jump into one using a web link. It is a simple way to stay connected without needing an iPhone.

Does this make you more likely to use FaceTime, or do you prefer other apps?
